attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated without hedging.

semantics.note: The universal scope ('every single AI service you use') and the causal link ('as a result') are both kept. Classing it as causal fits the wording.

contract.note: The plain reading (paid gen-AI services, service-level losses caused by compute subsidy, Q1 2026) is an ordinary reading. The result depends on which services count, e.g. image tools, and on the accounting basis, which the speaker never stated.

evidence.note: Secondary report of a CEO interview calling Midjourney profitable. It is a possible counterexample, but it gives no period, no basis and no service-level accounts, and image generation may be out of scope.

Anthropic S-1, filed before the evaluation date, shows a consolidated Q1 2026 operating loss. Company-wide compute spending includes R&D, so it does not show subscription-service losses caused by subsidy.

reviews.rationale: The claim is universal and causal. The packet has no service-level revenue and inference-cost figures for any in-scope service. Anthropic's consolidated loss is context only. Midjourney's reported profitability lacks the period, basis and scope needed to contradict under the contract. The evidence settles neither side.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The antecedent (OpenAI can't pay for the compute) is kept. The debt figures are supporting premises from the 'because' clause and are carried over accurately.

contract.note: Reading 'dies' as insolvency or ceasing to be a going concern is the ordinary plain reading. The trigger requires a documented payment failure. No deadline was given.

evidence.note: Oracle's own disclosure of its 2026 debt and equity plan. It bears on how the financing premise is classified, not on the antecedent or the outcome.
10-K says no ATM shares were sold by May 31, 2026, which undercuts a premise in the surrounding text. It shows no OpenAI payment failure and no Oracle insolvency.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast. The packet shows no OpenAI failure to pay Stargate obligations, so the antecedent is unknown and the claim is not scored. No conclusive event meets the early-resolution rule. The financing evidence bears only on the side premises.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. The WSJ quote that follows it is cited support, not the claim itself.

semantics.note: Keeps 'every single month for three years' and the idea that users were allowed to burn more than they paid.

contract.note: Reading 'allowing users' as permitting heavy users to cost more than their fee is fair and ordinary. Using actual costs rather than retail token prices fits the subsidy context. The three-year window is approximate.

evidence.note: Contemporaneous report of heavy-user losses in early 2023, at or just before the start of the window. It says nothing about later months.
GitHub's April 2026 statement that it absorbed rising inference costs is a company disclosure. It gives no per-user costs set against fees and does not cover the whole interval.
Second-hand report from October 2023 that Copilot was profitable. Overall profitability does not rule out heavy users being subsidised, so under the contract it does not contradict.

reviews.rationale: The evidence covers early 2023 and April 2026 but nothing month by month in between, so continuity over three years is not established. The October 2023 profitability report does not meet the contradiction condition. The packet does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The Friar quote before it is reported material, but the dependency claim is his.

semantics.note: The core claim is that Oracle's solvency depends on OpenAI passing $280B in revenue. The 'warning sign' part is evaluative rhetoric that the drafter folded in, which is acceptable.

contract.note: Reading 'critical' as necessary is a fair reading in a sentence about not running out of money, but it is the speaker's word choice that decides the result: if 'critical' only means 'important', the test would be much weaker. The contract marks this flag false, but the reading does decide the result.

evidence.note: CNBC report that the $280B figure is OpenAI's 2030 target. It shows the figure exists but says nothing about Oracle's dependence on it.
Oracle's own disclosure of operating cash flow, its financing, and its claim that new AI contracts are funded by customer prepayments. This is a company statement, not a complete solvency analysis.

reviews.rationale: No payment schedule or cash-flow analysis links OpenAI's revenue threshold to Oracle's ability to meet its obligations. Oracle's disclosures are context and do not show it would survive below the threshold. The evidence does not settle the claimed dependence.
